options.why: Passive income clubs with the higher-earning parent — the mother — after the ₹1,500 exemption. Chess prize money is income from the minor's skill and talent, which section 64(1A) leaves out of clubbing altogether.

items.scenario: A fourteen-year-old earns ₹2.4 lakh in bank interest on money gifted by grandparents, and ₹3 lakh in prize money from national-level chess tournaments. The father's income is ₹30 lakh and the mother's ₹42 lakh.

items.stem: How much of the loss reduces his other income this year?

options.text: The full ₹5.6 lakh, since let-out property interest has no ceiling
options.misconception: confuses the uncapped interest deduction with uncapped set-off
options.why: Both statements are true separately and the trap is joining them. Interest is fully deductible in computing the property loss; the loss then hits the two-lakh gate on its way to the salary.

options.text: ₹2 lakh now; ₹3.6 lakh carries forward against house property income for eight years
options.why: Section 71(3A) caps the inter-head set-off at two lakh however large the computed loss. The remainder is not lost — it carries forward — but it waits for house property income, which for many taxpayers means it waits a long time.

options.text: Nothing, because losses from let-out property cannot touch salary at all
options.misconception: overreads the cap into a prohibition
options.why: The set-off exists — section 71 permits it — and the 2017 amendment only capped it. Two lakh of this loss reduces the salary income this year.

options.text: ₹2 lakh now, with the balance carrying forward against any head of income
options.misconception: carries the loss forward with wider set-off rights than it left with
options.why: Carried-forward house property loss narrows, not widens — in later years it meets only house property income. The inter-head window exists in year one alone, capped.

items.scenario: An individual's let-out property produces a loss of ₹5.6 lakh this year, driven by home loan interest. His salary income is ₹28 lakh, and he expects the whole loss to reduce his salary tax this year.

items.stem: In which year is the ₹22 lakh deductible?

options.text: Next year — the due-date escape does not apply to MSME dues, so payment year governs
options.why: Clause (h) was built without the proviso that rescues other 43B items. The February bill on 30-day terms was payable beyond the MSMED window at the year end, so the deduction waits for the year of actual payment, the return's due date notwithstanding.

options.text: This year, since payment preceded the due date of filing the return
options.misconception: applies the general 43B proviso to the one clause carved out of it
options.why: The proviso's absence for clause (h) is the whole design — Parliament wanted MSMEs paid in days, not by October. The familiar rule is the trap laid for the well-prepared.

options.text: This year, because the liability was incurred when the goods were supplied
options.misconception: answers from the mercantile system that 43B overrides
options.why: Accrual is exactly what section 43B suspends for its listed sums. Incurring the liability starts the story; only payment finishes it.

options.text: Never, as delayed MSME payments are disallowed permanently as a penalty
options.misconception: converts a timing provision into a permanent disallowance
options.why: Section 43B defers, it does not confiscate. The deduction arrives with the payment year — the cost of delay is timing and the MSMED interest, not the deduction itself.

items.scenario: At 31 March a trader owes ₹22 lakh to a registered micro enterprise for goods supplied in February on 30-day terms. He pays on 25 July, well before filing his return on 31 October, and claims the deduction this year, citing the familiar rule that payment before the return's due date preserves it.

items.stem: What consideration does section 50C adopt for each sale?

options.text: ₹100 lakh and ₹96 lakh — the stamp value always prevails when higher
options.misconception: applies the deeming without the tolerance band
options.why: The 110 per cent tolerance exists exactly for genuine small gaps like the first sale. Deeming there taxes a difference Parliament chose to ignore.

options.text: ₹92 lakh and ₹88 lakh — the second sale is deemed at exactly 110 per cent
options.misconception: caps the deeming at the tolerance line instead of the stamp value
options.why: The tolerance is a gate, not a ceiling. Once crossed, the full stamp value of ₹96 lakh becomes the consideration; ₹88 lakh is only where the gate stood.

options.text: ₹92 lakh for the first sale; ₹96 lakh for the second
options.why: The first sale's stamp value of ₹100 lakh sits within 110 per cent of ₹92 lakh (₹101.2 lakh), so the tolerance protects the actual price. The second sale's ₹96 lakh exceeds 110 per cent of ₹80 lakh (₹88 lakh), so the deeming replaces the consideration in full — not merely the excess.

options.text: ₹92 lakh and ₹80 lakh — actual consideration governs capital gains
options.misconception: ignores the deeming provision entirely
options.why: Section 50C exists because understated property prices are the oldest trick in the book. Outside the tolerance, the stamp value is the consideration whether or not more money moved.

items.scenario: An individual sells a plot for ₹92 lakh. The stamp duty authority values it at ₹100 lakh for registration. In a second sale the same year, another plot fetches ₹80 lakh against a stamp value of ₹96 lakh.

items.stem: What is the consequence in the firm's computation?

options.text: The full ₹20 lakh is disallowed until the default is made good
options.misconception: applies the old full-disallowance rule or the non-resident clause
options.why: Hundred per cent disallowance is the pre-2014 history of this clause and remains the rule for payments abroad under 40(a)(i). For residents, Parliament softened it to thirty.

options.text: ₹6 lakh is disallowed permanently as the price of the default
options.misconception: reads a timing disallowance as a forfeiture
options.why: The clause's second limb restores the amount in the payment year. The cost of default is deferral and interest under the TDS chapter, not permanent loss.

options.text: ₹6 lakh is disallowed this year, and returns as a deduction in the year the TDS is paid
options.why: Section 40(a)(ia) disallows thirty per cent of the sum on which tax went undeducted, and the disallowance is temporary — the year the tax is finally deposited, the thirty per cent comes back. Genuineness of the expense never enters this section's arithmetic.

options.text: Nothing is disallowed, since the expense is genuine and evidenced
options.misconception: treats genuineness as answering a withholding default
options.why: The section polices deduction of tax, not the truth of the expense. The most genuine payment in the books still loses thirty per cent for the default.

items.scenario: A firm pays ₹20 lakh as contract charges to a resident contractor during the year and deducts no tax at source. The books are otherwise clean and the expense is genuine and fully evidenced.

items.stem: How much 54EC exemption does she actually get?

options.text: ₹65 lakh — the whole land gain, since she invested more than that
options.misconception: accepts the asset gate but misses the monetary cap
options.why: Right asset, right window, but the section counts only fifty lakh of the investment. The remaining ₹15 lakh of gain is taxed at the long-term rate.

options.text: ₹1.35 crore — the full amount invested within six months
options.misconception: reads the six-month window as the only condition
options.why: Timing is necessary, not sufficient. The asset-class gate and the fifty-lakh cap operate on top of it, and here they cut the claim by more than half.

options.text: ₹1 crore — fifty lakh against each of the two gains
options.misconception: applies the cap per asset instead of per financial year
options.why: The fifty-lakh ceiling is on investment in the financial year, not per transfer — and the share gain was never eligible, whatever the cap.

options.text: ₹50 lakh, against the land gain only
options.why: Two gates close most of the claim: 54EC covers only gains from land or building, so the share gain is out entirely, and the investment that counts is capped at fifty lakh in a financial year. Of the ₹65 lakh land gain, ₹50 lakh is exempt and the rest is taxed.

items.scenario: An individual sells listed shares in June, realising a long-term gain of ₹70 lakh, and a plot of land in July, realising a long-term gain of ₹65 lakh. In September she invests ₹1.35 crore in NHAI-class 54EC bonds and claims exemption for both gains in full.

items.stem: What does opting into 115BAA actually cost the company?

options.text: All three go — the incentives are surrendered, and with MAT inapplicable the MAT credit lapses
options.why: The concessional rate is bought by giving up the specified incentives, unabsorbed additional depreciation and profit-linked deductions among them. MAT not applying sounds like relief but also means the accumulated credit has nothing to set against — which is why companies with large credits often wait before opting.

options.text: Only a timing cost — the option can be dropped in a lean year and retaken later
options.misconception: treats an irrevocable option as an annual election
options.why: Once exercised, the option applies to that year and all subsequent years. Walking out in a lean year is exactly the flexibility the section withholds.

options.text: The deductions go, but the MAT credit survives to offset the new liability
options.misconception: keeps a credit born of a levy the company has left
options.why: MAT credit exists to smooth MAT paid against regular tax. Under 115BAA there is no MAT at all, and the credit cannot cross into a regime that never charges it.

options.text: Nothing — the lower rate and the incentives run together
options.misconception: prices the option at zero
options.why: Parliament's bargain is rate for incentives. A company keeping both would make the regular regime pointless for everyone.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company weighing the 115BAA option has ₹12 crore of unabsorbed additional depreciation, sizeable MAT credit carried forward, and a claim under a profit-linked deduction. The CFO believes the company can opt in, enjoy twenty-two per cent, and still use all three.

items.stem: How much revenue does the manufacturer recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Revenue for the 60 per cent the agent has sold to end customers
options.why: Control of consigned goods does not pass on despatch — the agent can return them and holds them for the manufacturer. Control passes when the agent sells to a customer, so only those units have satisfied a performance obligation under Ind AS 115.

options.text: Revenue spread evenly over the consignment period
options.misconception: converts a point-in-time obligation into an over-time one without meeting any criterion
options.why: Over-time recognition needs one of the Ind AS 115 criteria — the customer consuming the benefit as the entity performs, or the entity creating an asset the customer controls. A consignment of finished goods meets none of them.

options.text: Revenue for the full despatch, since the goods have left the premises
options.misconception: treats despatch as sale, the recognition trigger Ind AS 115 replaced
options.why: Despatch moves the goods, not control. The agent has no obligation to pay for unsold units and can return them, so the manufacturer still controls them.

options.text: No revenue until the agent remits the money
options.misconception: uses receipt of cash as the recognition trigger
options.why: Collection is a separate matter from recognition. Once control of a unit has passed to an end customer, the obligation is satisfied whether or not the agent has remitted.

items.scenario: A manufacturer despatches goods to a consignment agent on 28 March 2026. The agent holds the goods, can return any unsold units, and sells to end customers on the manufacturer's behalf. By 31 March the agent has sold 60 per cent of the units to customers.

items.stem: Which inventory cost formula does Ind AS 2 not permit?

options.text: Specific identification
options.misconception: forgets the formula required for non-interchangeable items
options.why: Specific identification is not merely permitted — it is required where items are not ordinarily interchangeable, such as goods segregated for a specific project.

options.text: LIFO
options.why: Ind AS 2 allows specific identification for non-interchangeable items, and FIFO or weighted average for the rest. LIFO is expressly not an option — in a rising price environment it books the newest, dearest cost first and leaves inventory at stale values.

options.text: Weighted average
options.misconception: assumes averaging is imprecise and therefore barred
options.why: Weighted average is the other permitted formula for interchangeable items.

options.text: FIFO
options.misconception: confuses the permitted default with the prohibited formula
options.why: FIFO is one of the two formulas permitted for interchangeable items.

items.stem: Does the company control the investee under Ind AS 110?

options.text: No, but the investee is a joint venture
options.misconception: mislabels one-sided board control as joint control
options.why: Joint control requires unanimous consent of the sharing parties over relevant activities. A right to appoint four of seven directors is unilateral, not shared.

options.text: No, the 45 per cent holding gives significant influence and equity accounting
options.misconception: stops at the shareholding percentage and applies the associate test
options.why: Significant influence is the fallback when control is absent. Here the board rights give actual power, so the investee is a subsidiary and is consolidated.

options.text: No, because control requires holding more than half the voting power
options.misconception: equates control with majority shareholding
options.why: Majority voting power is one route to power, not the definition of it. Ind AS 110 was written precisely to catch control held through other means.

options.text: Yes — it has power through the board rights, variable returns, and the link between them
options.why: All three elements of control are present. Power does not have to come from a majority of shares; a contractual right to appoint the majority of the board directs the relevant activities just as effectively.

items.scenario: A company holds 45 per cent of the voting shares of an investee. A shareholders' agreement gives it the contractual right to appoint four of the seven directors, and its returns vary with the investee's performance.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 109 require instead?

options.text: An allowance once a receivable is more than 90 days overdue
options.misconception: imports the banking overdue norms into financial reporting
options.why: Ninety days is a prudential banking classification, not an Ind AS measurement rule. There is a rebuttable presumption of default at 90 days past due, but the allowance exists long before that.

options.text: A 12-month expected credit loss allowance unless credit risk has increased significantly
options.misconception: applies the general staging model where the simplified approach governs
options.why: The two-stage general model applies to loans and debt investments. Trade receivables take the simplified approach, which is lifetime losses without a staging test.

options.text: A lifetime expected credit loss allowance on trade receivables from initial recognition
options.why: Ind AS 109 replaced the incurred-loss model with expected credit losses, recognised before any default. For trade receivables the simplified approach removes the staging debate entirely — the allowance is always lifetime expected losses.

options.text: The company's policy is compliant, since losses should not be anticipated
options.misconception: defends the incurred-loss model the standard replaced
options.why: Waiting for the loss event is exactly what Ind AS 109 abolished. Expected losses are an estimate of the future, made from the first day the receivable exists.

items.scenario: A company recognises a loss allowance on trade receivables only when a customer has actually defaulted, on the ground that anything earlier would be providing for losses that have not happened.

items.stem: Where does the ₹8 crore gain go under Ind AS 103?

options.text: Other comprehensive income, accumulated in capital reserve
options.why: This is the Indian carve-out. IFRS 3 takes a bargain purchase gain to profit or loss; Ind AS 103 routes it through other comprehensive income into capital reserve, keeping a purchase discount out of earnings.

options.text: Reduced from the values of the assets acquired
options.misconception: treats the gain as a measurement error to be spread over assets
options.why: Reassessment happens first, and this scenario says it already has. Once the measurements stand, the difference is a recognised gain, not an allocation.

options.text: Deferred and amortised to profit or loss over five years
options.misconception: invents an amortisation treatment the standard does not contain
options.why: Nothing in Ind AS 103 spreads a bargain purchase gain over time. It is recognised at once, in other comprehensive income.

options.text: Profit or loss immediately
options.misconception: applies the IFRS 3 treatment where the Indian carve-out differs
options.why: Correct under IFRS 3, and the classic trap in an Ind AS paper. The carve-out exists precisely because recognising acquisition-day gains in earnings was thought unsuitable.

items.scenario: A company acquires a business for ₹70 crore when the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is ₹78 crore. After reassessing the identification and measurement, the ₹8 crore difference remains.

items.stem: How is revenue recognised on the two contracts?

options.text: Both at a point in time, on completion of each project
options.misconception: defaults everything to completion without testing the over-time criteria
options.why: The factory meets two routes into over-time recognition. Deferring it all to completion would misstate every year the construction spans.

options.text: Both over time, because construction contracts are always percentage-of-completion
options.misconception: carries the old AS 7 reflex into a standard that tests criteria, not contract type
options.why: There is no contract-type rule any more. Each contract is tested against the para 35 criteria, and the flats fail them — alternative use exists and payment rights do not.

options.text: The flats over time, since forty units means performance is continuous
options.misconception: reads continuous physical work as continuous transfer of control
options.why: Continuous effort is not the test — continuous transfer of control is. Buyers of the flats control nothing until handover, however steadily the builder works.

options.text: The factory over time; the flats at a point in time on handover
options.why: The factory sits on the customer's land — the customer controls the asset as it is built — and there is an enforceable right to payment for work to date, so the over-time criteria are met. The flats have an alternative use to the builder and carry no right to payment before handover, so control passes only then.

items.scenario: A builder constructs a customised factory on the customer's own land. The contract entitles the builder to payment for work completed to date, including a reasonable margin, if the customer terminates. A separate contract in the same year is for 40 identical flats built on the builder's land, saleable to anyone, with payment only on handover.

items.stem: Is a provision recognised at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Yes, as a contingent liability measured at ₹18 crore
options.misconception: recognises a contingent liability instead of disclosing it
options.why: Contingent liabilities are never recognised on the balance sheet; they are disclosed. Recognition and disclosure are different acts, and this scenario earns neither a provision nor, before any obligation exists, a disclosure.

options.text: Yes, because the decision is formal, detailed and reliably costed
options.misconception: treats an internal decision as the obligating event
options.why: Formality and a reliable estimate satisfy other conditions, but the first condition — a present obligation — fails. An unannounced plan binds nobody, not even the company.

options.text: No — without announcement or commencement there is no constructive obligation yet
options.why: A provision needs a present obligation from a past event. A board decision alone creates none: the company can still change its mind. The obligating event arrives only when the plan is announced to those affected or implementation begins, creating a valid expectation.

options.text: No, but the ₹18 crore must be set aside as a reserve out of profits
options.misconception: substitutes an appropriation of profit for a liability test
options.why: Reserves are appropriations decided by the company; provisions are liabilities decided by the standard's criteria. Failing the liability test does not create an appropriation requirement.

items.scenario: In March 2026 a company's board resolves to close a loss-making division next year. The plan is detailed and costed at ₹18 crore, but nothing has been announced to anyone affected by 31 March.

items.stem: How is the ₹8 crore accounted for?

options.text: Deferred as a prepaid expense and spread over five years
options.misconception: parks a component of PPE in prepayments
options.why: Spreading over five years is the right rhythm but the wrong home. The cost belongs in the vessel's carrying amount as a component with its own depreciation, not in current assets.

options.text: Charged to profit or loss, since an inspection is maintenance
options.misconception: files a capitalisable overhaul under routine repairs
options.why: Day-to-day servicing is expensed. A five-yearly dry-docking required for the licence is not servicing — it purchases five more years of operation, which is an asset.

options.text: Capitalised, but nothing derecognised because the old inspection was never recognised separately
options.misconception: lets poor componentisation at purchase block the derecognition
options.why: The standard anticipates exactly this and directs an estimate — the cost of the new inspection is the indication of what the old one was. Skipping derecognition would carry two inspections in one carrying amount.

options.text: Capitalised into the vessel, with the ₹1.5 crore remnant of the old inspection derecognised
options.why: A major inspection that is a condition of operating is a component in its own right. The new cost enters the carrying amount and is depreciated to the next dry-docking; the previous inspection's remnant leaves, and Ind AS 16 says this holds even where that cost was never separately identified at acquisition.

items.scenario: A shipping company must dry-dock each vessel every five years as a condition of its licence. This year's dry-docking of one vessel costs ₹8 crore. The previous dry-docking, done by the seller before the vessel was purchased, was never identified as a separate component; its estimated remaining carrying amount is ₹1.5 crore.

items.stem: How are the two items translated at the year end?

options.text: The receivable moves to ₹86, with the gain deferred until the customer actually pays
options.misconception: holds unrealised exchange gains out of income
options.why: Ind AS 21 recognises exchange differences on monetary items in profit or loss in the period they arise. Realisation is not the trigger; the rate movement is.

options.text: The receivable moves to ₹86 with a ₹8 lakh gain in profit or loss; the inventory stays at ₹82
options.why: The receivable is a monetary item — a right to receive currency — so it takes the closing rate and its difference goes to profit or loss. Inventory is non-monetary at historical cost, frozen at the transaction-date rate, subject only to its own NRV test.

options.text: Both move to ₹86, since both arose in dollars
options.misconception: translates everything foreign at closing rate
options.why: The currency of origin is not the test; the monetary character is. Restating inventory for exchange movements would revalue an asset the standard keeps at cost.

options.text: Both stay at ₹82, the rate at which they were recorded
options.misconception: freezes monetary items at the transaction rate
options.why: A dollar claim is worth what dollars are worth today. Leaving the receivable at ₹82 hides a real ₹8 lakh of value the reporting date has already delivered.

items.scenario: At 31 March a company holds a $200,000 trade receivable booked at ₹82, and inventory imported during the year for $100,000 also booked at ₹82. The closing rate is ₹86.

items.stem: Can the internally built brand be recognised?

options.text: No — internally generated brands are expressly barred from recognition
options.why: Ind AS 38 bars internally generated brands, mastheads and customer lists because their cost cannot be told apart from the cost of growing the business as a whole. The rivals' brands sit on balance sheets because they were bought — a transaction gives them a cost.

options.text: Yes, at fair value determined by an independent brand valuer
options.misconception: substitutes valuation for the prohibited recognition
options.why: A valuer can price what the standard will not recognise. Fair value is a measurement basis, and measurement never arises for an asset barred at the recognition step.

options.text: No, but the ₹12 crore can be carried as deferred marketing expenditure
options.misconception: parks a barred asset under a different label
options.why: Deferred expenditure with no recognisable asset behind it is the same asset in a different coat. The spending is expense in the year it is incurred.

options.text: Yes, at the ₹12 crore actually spent, since the cost is reliably measured
options.misconception: treats measurable spending as satisfying recognition
options.why: The bar is not about measurement difficulty alone; it is absolute for these items. The standard refuses the asset however tidy the cost records are.

items.scenario: A consumer company spends ₹12 crore during the year building its flagship brand through design, promotion and market position, and its finance team proposes recognising the brand as an intangible asset, pointing to rival companies whose acquired brands sit on their balance sheets.

items.stem: Which segments must be reported separately?

options.text: Only the first two, since only they cross ten per cent
options.misconception: stops at the thresholds and misses the 75 per cent floor
options.why: The thresholds select; the floor then checks coverage. Passing the first test with 72 per cent coverage is precisely the case the second test exists to catch.

options.text: The first two on the thresholds, plus one more until reported segments cover 75 per cent
options.why: Crossing any ten per cent test makes the first two reportable, but para 15 adds a floor — reportable segments must carry at least 75 per cent of external revenue. At 72 per cent the entity keeps adding segments, threshold or not, until the floor is met.

options.text: Only the first, since it alone dominates the entity's results
options.misconception: reports the dominant segment and discards the tests entirely
options.why: Dominance is not the criterion — the ten per cent tests are, and the second segment crosses them. One-segment reporting would fail both the thresholds and the floor.

options.text: All four, because segments identified internally must all be reported
options.misconception: equates operating segments with reportable ones
options.why: Identification and reportability are different steps. Small segments can be aggregated or folded into an all-other column once the floor is satisfied.

items.scenario: A company has four operating segments. Segment revenues including inter-segment sales are ₹700, ₹150, ₹90 and ₹60 crore against a combined ₹1,000 crore. Only the first two cross any ten per cent test. External revenue of the first two together is 72 per cent of the entity's external revenue.

items.stem: How is the loan classified at 31 March?

options.text: Non-current, since the bank never actually demanded repayment
options.misconception: waits for the demand instead of testing the right
options.why: The test is the existence of the lender's right, not its exercise. A loan the bank could call today is current even if the bank stays friendly.

options.text: Split — current until the waiver date, non-current for the rest of the year
options.misconception: prorates a classification that is binary at one date
options.why: Classification speaks as at the reporting date, one date and one answer. There is no part-year presentation of the same liability.

options.text: Current — the waiver came after the reporting date, when the right to defer did not exist
options.why: Classification is tested on conditions existing at the reporting date. On 31 March the bank could demand repayment, so no right to defer settlement existed; the April waiver is a non-adjusting later event, disclosed rather than reclassified.

options.text: Non-current — the waiver arrived before the accounts were approved and restores the schedule
options.misconception: lets an approval-date event rewrite a reporting-date condition
options.why: The approval date matters for what is disclosed, not for what existed. At the year end the company stood exposed to demand, and the statements report the year end.

items.scenario: A company breaches a debt-equity covenant on its ₹120 crore term loan as at 31 March, making the loan repayable on demand. On 20 April, before the accounts are approved, the bank issues a formal waiver and confirms the original 2030 repayment schedule stands.

items.stem: How does Ind AS 7 classify the two flows for this company?

options.text: Interest paid as financing; interest received as investing
options.why: The Indian carve-out removed the IFRS options — for an entity that is not a financial institution, interest paid belongs to financing and interest received to investing, full stop. The accountant's rule is real IFRS and wrong Ind AS.

options.text: Both as operating, since IAS 7 permits it and Ind AS follows IFRS
options.misconception: assumes convergence means identity
options.why: Ind AS converges with carve-outs, and this is a named one. The options were removed precisely to make Indian cash flow statements comparable to each other.

options.text: Both as financing, since both concern borrowing and lending money
options.misconception: nets the two sides of treasury into one classification
options.why: Paying for capital and earning on deposits are different activities. The statement's whole purpose is keeping those directions apart.

options.text: The classification is the entity's accounting policy choice, applied consistently
options.misconception: preserves the choice the carve-out abolished
options.why: Consistency was IFRS's condition on a choice that Ind AS does not offer. For non-financial entities there is one answer, not a policy.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company paid ₹18 crore of interest on term loans and received ₹2 crore of interest on surplus deposits. Its accountant, trained on IFRS materials, classifies both as operating cash flows, noting that IAS 7 permits it.

items.stem: Which leases can stay off the balance sheet?

options.text: The warehouse and the laptops — nine months is under twelve
options.misconception: counts the months and misses the purchase-option bar
options.why: A lease with a purchase option is excluded from the short-term exemption by definition — the option signals the asset may never come back, which is not a short-term arrangement in substance.

options.text: Only the laptops — the warehouse's purchase option defeats the short-term exemption, and three years is simply long
options.why: The short-term election is barred where a purchase option exists, whatever the term's length, so the warehouse comes on. Three years of office space is outside every exemption. The laptops ride the low-value election, which is available asset by asset.

options.text: All three, by electing the exemptions across the portfolio
options.misconception: stretches two narrow elections into a general escape
options.why: The elections cover only what their conditions cover. Ind AS 116 exists because keeping ordinary leases off balance sheets is the outcome standard-setters buried.

options.text: None — Ind AS 116 abolished off-balance-sheet leases entirely
options.misconception: overcorrects past both stated exemptions
options.why: The two elections are in the standard's own text. The laptops are the case they were written for.

items.scenario: A company signs three agreements — a nine-month lease of a warehouse with an option to buy it at the term's end, a three-year lease of office space, and one-year leases of forty laptops of modest value. The CFO wants every one of them kept off the balance sheet.

items.stem: Is the impairment correct?

options.text: No impairment now, but the ₹15 crore excess of value in use must be written up as a gain
options.misconception: turns an impairment test into a revaluation
options.why: Ind AS 36 only writes down. Headroom above carrying amount is simply the absence of impairment; writing assets up is a different policy under a different standard.

options.text: No — recoverable amount is ₹85 crore, above carrying amount, so there is no impairment
options.why: Recoverable amount takes the higher of the two measures, and value in use at ₹85 crore beats fair value less costs of disposal at ₹70 crore. The entity is not obliged to sell; an asset worth more in use than on the block recovers its carrying amount by being used.

options.text: Yes — an asset cannot be carried above what it would fetch in the market
options.misconception: treats fair value as a ceiling on carrying amount
options.why: That ceiling belongs to assets held for sale. For assets held for use, Ind AS 36 lets value in use answer, precisely because a business often earns more from a plant than a buyer would pay for it.

options.text: Yes, but the loss is ₹5 crore, impairing down to the average of the two measures
options.misconception: splits the difference instead of taking the higher
options.why: Nothing in the standard averages the two. The comparison is carrying amount against the higher measure, and ₹80 crore against ₹85 crore needs no write-down at all.

items.scenario: A plant is carried at ₹80 crore. A broker would pay ₹70 crore for it net of costs, and the discounted cash flows from continuing to run it come to ₹85 crore. The accountant books a ₹10 crore impairment loss, reasoning that the market has spoken and the plant cannot be sold for its carrying amount.

items.stem: Which balances are retranslated at ₹84?

options.text: The receivable and the advance — both arose from cash actually paid or receivable
options.misconception: tests where the balance came from instead of how it settles
options.why: The advance began as cash but ends as goods. Settlement in something other than a fixed amount of currency is what makes it non-monetary, however cash-flavoured its origin.

options.text: All three — every foreign currency balance is restated at closing
options.misconception: retranslates by currency instead of by monetary character
options.why: Para 23 splits the balance sheet by nature, not by currency. Restating inventory and advances manufactures exchange differences on items that will never turn into dollars.

options.text: None, holding all items at ₹80 until realised, with differences booked on settlement
options.misconception: defers monetary retranslation to settlement
options.why: For monetary items the standard books the difference each reporting date, realised or not. Waiting for settlement understates a ₹8 crore gain the year-end position already holds.

options.text: Only the receivable — the inventory and the goods-advance are non-monetary and stay at ₹80
options.why: The receivable is a right to receive fixed currency units — monetary, closing rate, gain to profit or loss. Inventory is a thing, not a claim to currency. The advance, because it will be settled by delivery of goods rather than refund of cash, carries no right to currency units and stays frozen at the rate it was paid.

items.scenario: At year-end an Indian company holds three dollar balances from when the dollar was ₹80: a $2 million trade receivable, inventory that cost $1 million, and a $0.5 million advance paid to a supplier against future delivery of goods. The closing rate is ₹84.

items.stem: As auditor, what do you require before the report is signed?

options.text: A written representation from the CFO that the banks have been informed separately
options.misconception: routes a reporting defect into a representation
options.why: Whom the bankers heard from privately has no bearing on what the statements must say to every reader. And a representation is never sufficient evidence on its own, least of all about a disclosure that is visibly missing.

options.text: Disclosure of the material uncertainty in the notes to the financial statements themselves
options.why: Ind AS 1 puts the disclosure duty on the financial statements when management is aware of material uncertainties over going concern. The directors' report is not audited to the same standard and is not where SA 570's dedicated section can point. Without the note the statements are misstated, and the opinion — not just a paragraph — is what changes.

options.text: Nothing further, since the auditor's own going concern section will inform readers
options.misconception: uses the auditor's report to carry management's disclosure duty
options.why: The auditor's section draws attention to the note; it does not replace it. Where the note is absent, the statements are wrong and the response is a modified opinion, not a louder auditor's paragraph.

options.text: A more detailed description in the directors' report, cross-referenced from the audit report
options.misconception: accepts other-information disclosure as a substitute for the note
options.why: The directors' report is other information. A cross-reference from the audit report cannot cure an omission inside the statements — it would advertise the very gap it papers over.

items.scenario: A company has defaulted on its term loans and its net current liabilities are ₹80 crore. The CFO agrees a material uncertainty exists but proposes to describe it in the directors' report only, keeping the financial statements clean "so the bankers do not panic". The audit is in final review.

items.stem: What does section 188 require for this contract?

options.text: No approval, because buying fabric is the company's ordinary course of business
options.misconception: applies half the exemption and drops the arm's length half
options.why: The exemption needs both limbs: ordinary course and arm's length. An 8 per cent premium concedes the second limb, and one failed limb brings the section fully into play.

options.text: Only disclosure in the board's report, since the amount is below ₹50 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a disclosure threshold for the approval requirement
options.why: Thresholds decide when shareholders must approve on top of the board — they never reduce the requirement to disclosure alone. The board resolution is the floor, not the ceiling.

options.text: Approval of the Registrar of Companies before execution
options.misconception: sends a governance decision to the regulator
options.why: Section 188 keeps the decision inside the company — board, and shareholders where thresholds require. The Registrar receives filings; he does not approve contracts.

options.text: Board approval by resolution, with the interested director not participating
options.why: The counterparty is a related party and the pricing is not arm's length, so the ordinary- course-and-arm's-length exemption is unavailable. Section 188 then requires a board resolution — with shareholder approval as well if the prescribed thresholds are crossed — and the interested director stays out of the discussion and the vote.

items.scenario: A public company proposes to buy fabric worth ₹12 crore annually from a partnership in which a director's son is a partner, at prices about 8 per cent above the market, citing assured quality. The purchase committee asks what approvals the contract needs.

items.stem: Can the auditor accept this fee arrangement?

options.text: Yes, because fee structure is a private contract between auditor and client
options.misconception: places the engagement contract above the professional schedules
options.why: The Chartered Accountants Act sits over every engagement letter a member signs. A contract cannot authorise what the First Schedule defines as misconduct.

options.text: Yes, if the arrangement is disclosed to shareholders in the general meeting
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a prohibited arrangement
options.why: Disclosure cures conflicts that are permissible to hold. This one is prohibited outright; telling the shareholders about it only documents the misconduct.

options.text: No — fees contingent on results or based on a percentage of profits are prohibited
options.why: An auditor paid a share of the profit he certifies holds a stake in the number under audit. The First Schedule makes such fees professional misconduct, outside the narrow exceptions the Council has prescribed for specific engagements — statutory audit is not among them.

options.text: No, unless the percentage is capped at a maximum absolute amount
options.misconception: believes a ceiling converts a contingent fee into a fixed one
options.why: A capped percentage still rises and falls with the profits below the cap — the stake in the certified number remains. The defect is the linkage, not the size.

items.scenario: A client offers its statutory auditor a fee of 2 per cent of audited net profits, arguing it aligns the auditor's diligence with the company's success and is common for consultants.

items.stem: What does section 143(12) require of you?

options.text: Qualify the audit opinion and treat that as the report
options.misconception: treats the audit report to members as the fraud report to the Government
options.why: The opinion speaks to the financial statements; the 143(12) report is a separate filing to a different addressee with its own form and timeline. One cannot stand in for the other.

options.text: Report to the Central Government, routing it through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time
options.why: The fraud is by an employee against the company and crosses the one crore threshold, so the report goes to the Central Government in the prescribed manner — the board or audit committee gets the prescribed window to respond, and their comments travel with the report. Handling it quietly is not among the options the section leaves open.

options.text: Resign from the engagement to avoid association with the fraud
options.misconception: substitutes exit for the statutory duty
options.why: Resignation does not discharge section 143(12), and a resigning auditor still carries reporting duties. The Act wants the fraud reported, not the auditor gone.

options.text: Report it to the audit committee only, since internal fraud is a governance matter
options.misconception: applies the below-threshold route to an above-threshold fraud
options.why: Audit-committee-only reporting is the route for frauds under one crore. At ₹1.8 crore the section escalates the duty to the Central Government, and the committee cannot absorb it.

items.scenario: During the audit of a listed company you find that a purchase manager, colluding with a vendor, has siphoned ₹1.8 crore through inflated invoices over two years. Management asks you to note it internally and let the audit committee handle it quietly.

items.stem: Does section 135 apply?

options.text: Yes — the thresholds are alternatives, and the profit test is crossed
options.why: Any one of the three gates opens the section, and ₹6.2 crore of net profit is past the ₹5 crore gate. The committee, the policy and the 2 per cent of three-year average net profits all follow, however modest the balance sheet looks beside the other thresholds.

options.text: No, because CSR obligations attach only to listed companies
options.misconception: confuses CSR applicability with listing status
options.why: Section 135 never mentions listing. A private limited company past any threshold is as bound as a listed one.

options.text: Yes, but spending is optional so long as the board explains the shortfall
options.misconception: carries the old comply-or-explain regime past its amendment
options.why: Explain-only died with the 2021 amendments. Unspent money now transfers to an ongoing project account or a specified fund on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: No, because two of the three thresholds are not met
options.misconception: reads the alternative thresholds as cumulative
options.why: Requiring all three would confine CSR to giants. The section says net worth OR turnover OR profit, and one is enough.

items.scenario: A company has net worth ₹120 crore and turnover ₹800 crore, but its net profit for the immediately preceding year was ₹6.2 crore. The CFO argues CSR does not apply because the company is nowhere near the net worth or turnover thresholds.

items.stem: How do the two opinions in your report come out?

options.text: Unmodified on the financial statements; adverse on internal financial controls
options.why: Section 143(3)(i) makes controls a separate opinion answering a separate question. A material weakness draws an adverse controls opinion even where extended substantive work let the statements themselves be proved true and fair.

options.text: Unmodified on both, because the statements were ultimately proved right
options.misconception: lets the financial statement outcome absolve the controls
options.why: The controls opinion reports the state of the controls, not the state of the numbers. A material weakness that existed at the year end is reported whether or not it did damage.

options.text: The control failures go only in a management letter, not the audit report
options.misconception: demotes a statutory reporting duty to a private communication
options.why: The management letter supplements; it cannot substitute. Section 143(3)(i) puts the controls opinion in the report to members by force of statute.

options.text: Both must be qualified, since a control failure infects the statements
options.misconception: chains the two opinions together
options.why: The opinions can and do diverge. Broken controls raise the risk of misstatement; they do not prove one occurred, and here the substantive work proved otherwise.

items.scenario: Finalising a listed company's audit, you conclude the financial statements are true and fair, but testing showed the purchase-to-pay controls failed repeatedly and a material weakness exists at the year end.

items.stem: Which of the four falls foul of Clause 6?

options.text: The tender response, because concurrent audit was never offered to this firm personally
options.misconception: treats responding to an open invitation as uninvited approach
options.why: A tender is an invitation to everyone qualified. Answering an invitation is the opposite of soliciting; the mischief is approaching those who never asked.

options.text: The letter to the other firm, since work must come from clients directly
options.misconception: bars the one channel the clause expressly keeps open
options.why: Securing work from another chartered accountant in practice is a stated exception — professional sub-engagement is how overflow and specialisation have always moved.

options.text: All four, since each is an attempt to obtain professional work
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering every pursuit of work
options.why: The clause was never a vow of passivity. Its carve-outs exist precisely so that open, invited competition — tenders, empanelment, professional-to-professional requests — stays lawful.

options.text: Only the brochure mailing to the two hundred companies
options.why: Unsolicited circulars to prospective clients are the textbook form of solicitation the clause bars. The other three are its stated exceptions — responding to tenders, applying against announced empanelments, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice.

items.scenario: A firm of chartered accountants does four things in one quarter — mails brochures about its audit expertise to two hundred companies chosen from the registrar's records, responds to a public tender floated by a state bank for concurrent audit, applies against a public empanelment notice of a government corporation, and writes to another CA firm offering to take its overflow tax work.

items.stem: Does the proposed committee comply?

options.text: Yes, provided the committee's recommendations are ratified by the full board
options.misconception: cures defective composition with board ratification
options.why: Ratification cannot rebuild the committee. The statute regulates who deliberates, not just what emerges; a wrongly composed committee stays wrongly composed however its output is later blessed.

options.text: No, because the CFO's relative can never sit on any board committee
options.misconception: invents a blanket relative disqualification
options.why: Relationship to an officer affects independence classification, not committee membership as such. The defect is arithmetic — the independents lack a majority — not the presence of one related non-executive.

options.text: Yes — four exceeds the minimum of three, and independents are represented
options.misconception: checks the headcount and skips the majority condition
options.why: Representation is not the test; majority is. The minimum of three and the independent majority are separate conditions, and the second one fails here.

options.text: No — independent directors must form the majority, and two of four is not one
options.why: Section 177 requires a minimum of three directors with independents in the majority. Two of four fails the majority test, and a committee chaired by the managing director invites exactly the management dominance the composition rules exist to prevent.

items.scenario: A listed company proposes an audit committee of four directors — two independent, the managing director, and the CFO's brother as a non-executive director, chaired by the managing director. The company secretary certifies the composition complies with section 177.

items.stem: Does CARO 2020 apply to this company's audit?

options.text: No, since two of the three financial limits are within bounds
options.misconception: reads the cumulative exemption conditions as majority-satisfied
options.why: The exemption is conjunctive. Meeting two limits while breaking the third is simply breaking the conditions — the order does not average them.

options.text: Yes, but only the fraud and statutory dues clauses apply to private companies
options.misconception: invents a partial CARO for private companies
options.why: CARO has no reduced edition. Once applicable, the whole order applies; applicability is the only company-level question.

options.text: Yes — the revenue of ₹14 crore crosses the ten crore limit, and one breach is enough
options.why: The private-company exemption needs every limit honoured together — capital and reserves, borrowings, and revenue. Revenue at ₹14 crore breaks the ten crore ceiling, so the order applies with all its reporting clauses, whatever the other two figures say.

options.text: No, because CARO never applies to private companies
options.misconception: turns a conditional exemption into a blanket one
options.why: Private companies are exempt only inside the size limits. Beyond them, a private company answers every CARO clause a public one does.

items.scenario: A private limited company, not a holding or subsidiary of a public company, has paid-up capital and reserves of ₹80 lakh, bank borrowings that peaked at ₹95 lakh during the year, and revenue of ₹14 crore. Its auditor treats CARO 2020 as inapplicable since capital and borrowings are within a crore each.

items.stem: What is the most the company can distribute from current profits?

options.text: ₹28 crore, by adding the securities premium to distributable profit
options.misconception: treats securities premium as a free reserve
options.why: Premium is shareholders' capital contribution, usable only for the purposes section 52 lists. Distribution as dividend is not among them.

options.text: ₹3 crore — after depreciation and after setting off the carried-forward loss
options.why: Section 123 charges depreciation first (₹10 minus ₹3) and then requires previous losses and unabsorbed depreciation to be set off (₹7 minus ₹4), leaving ₹3 crore of distributable profit. The premium and revaluation balances watch from the sidelines.

options.text: ₹7 crore — depreciation must be provided, but old losses concern the balance sheet, not dividends
options.misconception: provides depreciation and skips the loss set-off
options.why: The set-off is a statutory pre-condition, not a presentation nicety. Paying dividends across an unabsorbed loss distributes capital dressed as income.

options.text: ₹18 crore, by drawing on the revaluation surplus
options.misconception: distributes an unrealised book write-up
options.why: A revaluation surplus is an accounting remeasurement, not realised profit. Dividending it hands out money the company never earned and may never see.

items.scenario: A company has current-year profit of ₹10 crore before providing ₹3 crore of depreciation, a brought-forward business loss of ₹4 crore, a securities premium of ₹25 crore, and a revaluation surplus of ₹15 crore. The board wants the largest lawful dividend.

items.stem: Can either proposal stand?

options.text: Neither — the cooling-off blocks any reappointment for five years, and the partner-linked firm is equally barred
options.why: Ten years is the ceiling, and the five-year cooling-off admits no short extensions — two years inside a barred window is barred. The fallback fails on the same section's own words: a firm with common partners as at the appointment date stands in the retiring firm's shoes.

options.text: The linked firm works, because it is a distinct legal entity
options.misconception: hides continuity behind a fresh registration
options.why: The statute anticipated the manoeuvre and named it: common partners carry the disqualification across the entity line.

options.text: The two-year extension works, since it is shorter than a term
options.misconception: reads the bar as prohibiting only full terms
options.why: The section bars appointment as auditor during the cooling-off, for any length. Slicing the term thin does not slip it through.

options.text: Both work if the audit committee certifies the firm's independence
options.misconception: lets a committee certify around a statutory bar
options.why: Independence certification supplements eligibility; it cannot manufacture it. A candidate the statute disqualifies stays disqualified with the finest certificate attached.

items.scenario: An audit firm completes its second five-year term at a listed company. The shareholders, pleased with its work, propose reappointing it for two more years only, arguing a short extension is not a fresh five-year term. As fallback they suggest a different firm in which three partners of the retiring firm hold a majority.

items.stem: Which of the CFO's three grounds survives section 138?

options.text: The first — private companies are outside internal audit requirements
options.misconception: reads section 138 as a public-company provision
options.why: The rule names private companies with their own thresholds. Two hundred crore of turnover is one of them, and this company is past it.

options.text: The third — the internal auditor must be a practising chartered accountant
options.misconception: narrows the section's deliberately wide eligibility
options.why: The provision expressly allows a cost accountant or such other professional as the board decides, and the rule adds that the appointee may be an employee. Parliament left the choice to the board.

options.text: None — the turnover line is crossed, in-house review is not internal audit, and the board may appoint a qualified employee
options.why: A private company past two hundred crore of turnover is squarely covered. A management team reviewing its own controls is self-review, not the independent function the section contemplates — but the section is generous on who: a chartered accountant, cost accountant or other professional, employee included, as the board decides.

options.text: The second — a documented monthly management review satisfies the requirement
options.misconception: accepts self-review as the audit of self
options.why: The reviewers report to the very management whose controls they review. Internal audit exists to stand outside that loop, reporting toward the audit committee.

items.scenario: A private company had turnover of ₹230 crore in the preceding year and no borrowings. The CFO resists appointing an internal auditor on three grounds — the company is private, its own accounts team reviews controls monthly, and in any case only chartered accountants can be internal auditors, which would mean hiring outside.

items.stem: Is the company covered, and can unspent CSR sit in the balance sheet?

options.text: Covered — the profit test alone triggers section 135 — and unspent amounts must move to the statutory accounts, not sit in the balance sheet
options.why: The three thresholds are alternatives; net profit of ₹9 crore against the five-crore line is enough on its own. Since the 2019 amendments, unspent money has mandated destinations — an unspent-CSR account within thirty days for ongoing projects, a Schedule VII fund within six months otherwise. A general reserve is neither.

options.text: Covered, but spending remains comply-or-explain, so unspent amounts need only a board explanation
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 regime as current law
options.why: Explanation alone was the original design. The amendments kept the explanation and added teeth — mandatory transfer of unspent amounts on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: Not covered — CSR needs at least two of the three thresholds crossed
options.misconception: reads "or" as "and"
options.why: The section strings its thresholds with "or". One gate open is enough, and the profit gate is open by four crore.

options.text: Covered, and the obligation is two per cent of the preceding year's ₹9 crore profit
options.misconception: computes on one year instead of the three-year average
options.why: Eligibility reads one year; the spend reads three. Two per cent applies to the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years, which smooths a lumpy profit like this one.

items.scenario: A company with turnover of ₹800 crore and net worth of ₹300 crore earned net profit of ₹9 crore in the immediately preceding year. Its CFO argues CSR does not apply since neither the net worth nor the turnover threshold is crossed. The board separately proposes that if CSR does apply, any unspent amount can be carried in the general balance sheet for later use.

items.stem: Can the company take the ₹7.2 lakh input tax credit?

options.text: No, and the goods must also be returned to the supplier
options.misconception: attaches a consequence to the goods when the defect is in the tax chain
options.why: The purchase itself is untouched — the goods are the company's. What fails is the credit; the company's remedy against the supplier is contractual, not a return of goods.

options.text: Yes — a valid invoice and receipt of goods complete the recipient's obligations
options.misconception: treats the recipient-side conditions as the whole test
options.why: That was the intuition under the old regime and it is the specific thing section 16(2)(c) rejects. The credit is of tax paid, and no tax was paid.

options.text: No — payment of the tax to the Government by the supplier is itself a condition
options.why: Section 16(2)(c) makes the supplier's actual payment a condition of the recipient's credit. Invoice, receipt and GSTR-2B appearance satisfy three conditions of five; all of them must hold together, and the missing one defeats the claim.

options.text: Yes, provisionally, reversible if the supplier stays in default for six months
options.misconception: recalls the provisional-credit mechanism that no longer exists
options.why: Provisional credit was removed from the law. Credit now follows GSTR-2B and the satisfied conditions, with no provisional window to occupy.

items.scenario: A company buys raw material worth ₹40 lakh plus ₹7.2 lakh GST, holds a valid tax invoice, has received the goods, and the invoice appears in its GSTR-2B. It then learns the supplier collected the tax but never deposited it with the Government.

items.stem: What is the GST position on these fees?

options.text: The company pays under reverse charge by debiting its input tax credit
options.misconception: discharges a reverse-charge liability through the credit ledger
options.why: Reverse charge must be paid through the cash ledger. The credit ledger can pay output tax on the company's own supplies, not the tax it owes as a recipient.

options.text: The company pays the GST under reverse charge, in cash
options.why: Legal services from an advocate to a business entity are notified under section 9(3), so the liability sits on the recipient. Reverse charge liability is discharged in cash — the company may then take credit of it, but cannot pay it out of credit.

options.text: The advocate should have charged GST on the bill
options.misconception: applies forward charge to a notified reverse-charge supply
options.why: For notified services the supplier neither charges nor collects. A bill without GST is the correct bill here; the tax travels on the company's own liability.

options.text: No GST arises, because legal services are exempt
options.misconception: stretches the small-recipient exemption to every recipient
options.why: The exemption covers advocates serving individuals and small business entities below the registration threshold. A ₹300 crore company is squarely outside it.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company with ₹300 crore turnover engages a senior advocate for a High Court matter and pays fees of ₹5 lakh. The advocate's bill shows no GST.

items.stem: Is registration required?

options.text: Yes, because every supplier of services must register from the first rupee
options.misconception: erases the threshold entirely for services
options.why: First-rupee registration applies to specific cases — inter-State taxable supply, e-commerce, reverse-charge recipients — not to services as a class.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹1.5 crore
options.misconception: mistakes the composition ceiling for the registration threshold
options.why: ₹1.5 crore is the composition scheme's eligibility ceiling — a choice available after registration, not a limit before it.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: applies the goods-only threshold to a service provider
options.why: The ₹40 lakh limit belongs to suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States. One rupee of service supply keeps the ₹20 lakh limit in charge.

options.text: Yes — the services threshold of ₹20 lakh is crossed
options.why: A supplier of services takes the ₹20 lakh aggregate turnover limit, and ₹25 lakh is past it. Registration follows, with tax on supplies from the effective date.

items.scenario: A management consultant in Madhya Pradesh, supplying only services within the State, reaches aggregate turnover of ₹25 lakh during the year and asks whether registration is now compulsory.

items.stem: Can he make this supply while remaining in the scheme?

options.text: Yes, because his turnover is within the ₹1.5 crore ceiling
options.misconception: treats the turnover ceiling as the only eligibility condition
options.why: The ceiling is one condition of several. The inter-State bar is separate, and breaching it disqualifies regardless of how modest the turnover is.

options.text: No — inter-State outward supply ends composition eligibility
options.why: Section 10(2) bars a composition taxpayer from inter-State outward supplies. Shipping to Maharashtra means leaving the scheme and paying tax as a regular taxpayer, with the compliance that follows.

options.text: Yes, paying IGST on this order at the composition rate
options.misconception: extends the composition rate across State lines
options.why: There is no composition IGST. The scheme is a local-trade bargain, and the levy it charges exists only for intra-State supply.

options.text: Yes, if the Maharashtra buyer arranges his own transport from Indore
options.misconception: locates the supply by who carries the goods
options.why: Place of supply follows the movement's termination for delivery, not who pays the transporter. Goods bound for Maharashtra make an inter-State supply either way.

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Indore, selling hardware with turnover of ₹90 lakh, receives a large order from a buyer in Maharashtra and intends to supply it under the composition scheme.

items.stem: Which of these amounts is not added in arriving at the assessable value?

options.text: The selling commission of $2,000
options.misconception: excludes all commissions instead of only the buying commission
options.why: Selling commission is paid for the seller's benefit and is expressly added. The carve-out is for buying commission alone.

options.text: None of them — all payments connected with the import are added
options.misconception: adds everything rather than testing each payment against the rule
options.why: The rule works addition by addition, and buying commission is its stated exception. Adding everything overstates the value and the duty with it.

options.text: The buying commission of $1,500
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) adds commissions and brokerage except buying commission. The importer's own agent works for the buyer, and paying him is part of the cost of buying, not part of the price of the goods.

options.text: The freight of $3,000
options.misconception: leaves transport out of a value that is built to the place of importation
options.why: Cost of transport to the place of importation is a Rule 10(2) addition. Assessable value is the landed value, and freight is part of landing the goods.

items.scenario: An importer's invoice shows goods at $50,000, selling commission of $2,000 paid to the exporter's agent, buying commission of $1,500 paid to the importer's own agent abroad, and freight of $3,000 to the Indian port.

items.stem: Can the credit still be taken?

options.text: No, because credit must be taken in the same month as the invoice
options.misconception: shrinks the statutory window to the invoice month
options.why: The law allows credit any time up to the section 16(4) date — often twenty months from an early-year invoice. The failure here is missing a generous window, not a same-month rule.

options.text: Yes, because the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed
options.misconception: reads the two limbs as alternatives that each keep the window open
options.why: The section takes the EARLIER of the two dates. An unfiled annual return cannot extend the November cut-off; it can only close the window sooner.

options.text: No — the window closed on 30 November 2026
options.why: The invoice belongs to financial year 2025-26, so section 16(4) shuts the credit at the thirtieth of November following that year's end. Discovery in December is discovery too late, however eligible the credit was on its merits.

options.text: Yes, at any time within four years, as with other indirect tax refunds
options.misconception: imports a limitation period from refund law into the credit provision
options.why: Refund limitation under section 54 is a different clock for a different claim. Credit has its own guillotine in section 16(4), and it is measured in months, not years.

items.scenario: During a December 2026 review, a company discovers an unclaimed input tax credit of ₹6 lakh on a supplier invoice dated 14 February 2026. All section 16(2) conditions are satisfied and the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed.

items.stem: What is the place of supply, and which tax applies?

options.text: Madhya Pradesh, because the buyer arranged the transport himself
options.misconception: lets who carries the goods decide the place of supply
options.why: Movement "whether by the supplier or the recipient" is within the same rule. The statute cares about the destination of the movement, not about whose truck it is.

options.text: Madhya Pradesh — an intra-State supply, since delivery was taken at the factory gate
options.misconception: fixes the place of supply where possession changed hands rather than where movement ends
options.why: Handing over at the gate is how the movement begins, not where it terminates. The section looks at where the goods are going for delivery to the recipient, which is Ahmedabad.

options.text: Gujarat, but as an intra-State supply of Gujarat attracting CGST and SGST
options.misconception: gets the place right and then misreads what inter-State means
options.why: Inter-State or intra-State compares the supplier's location with the place of supply. Supplier in Madhya Pradesh, place of supply Gujarat — that is inter-State, and IGST is the levy.

options.text: Gujarat — an inter-State supply attracting IGST
options.why: The supply involves movement of goods, and the movement terminates for delivery at the Ahmedabad plant. Section 10(1)(a) fixes the place of supply there, and Madhya Pradesh to Gujarat is inter-State, so IGST applies.

items.scenario: A dealer in Bhopal sells machinery to a buyer registered in Gujarat. The buyer sends its own truck, takes delivery at the Bhopal factory gate, and carries the machinery to its Ahmedabad plant.

items.stem: Who pays GST in March on the advance?

options.text: Neither, because no invoice has been issued by either
options.misconception: makes the invoice the sole trigger for both goods and services
options.why: For services the payment reaches back as a trigger on its own. The software company's liability arises in March with or without an invoice.

options.text: Both, since money received against a taxable supply is taxable when received
options.misconception: applies the services rule across the goods-services line
options.why: That was the position for goods only briefly. The notification removed advances on goods from the net after the compliance burden proved unworkable, and the asymmetry is now the tested point.

options.text: Only the manufacturer, since goods are tangible and the machine is identifiable
options.misconception: reverses the asymmetry
options.why: The rule runs the other way. Tangibility has nothing to do with it — the notification names goods as the excused side.

options.text: Only the software company — advances for services are taxable on receipt; for goods they are not
options.why: Time of supply for services reaches the earlier of invoice and payment, catching the advance in March. For goods, Notification 66/2017 confined the liability to invoice issue, so the manufacturer pays in May with the invoice.

items.scenario: On 20 March a machine manufacturer receives a ₹10 lakh advance against a machine to be delivered in May, and a software company receives a ₹10 lakh advance against an implementation project starting in May. Both are regular taxpayers.

items.stem: Which discount reduces the value of supply for GST?

options.text: The 2 per cent scheme discount, provided the dealer reverses the proportionate credit
options.why: It was agreed before the supplies, is linkable to specific invoices, and the recipient's credit reversal completes section 15(3)(b). The tax follows the price the parties had genuinely agreed all along.

options.text: Both, since both are genuine discounts actually passed on
options.misconception: treats commercial genuineness as the statutory test
options.why: Genuineness is necessary but the section demands prior agreement and invoice linkage. The goodwill discount was born after the supplies and fails at the first condition.

options.text: Neither, because post-supply discounts never reduce taxable value
options.misconception: reads the pre-supply agreement condition as banning all later discounts
options.why: The section exists precisely to allow post-supply discounts that were pre-agreed. What it shuts out is the discount invented after the event.

options.text: The goodwill discount, since it is unconditional and unilateral
options.misconception: rewards the discount with fewer strings as the cleaner deduction
options.why: Unconditional generosity is exactly what the section will not net off. The strings — prior agreement, linkage, reversal — are the qualification, not the disqualification.

items.scenario: A distributor agreement signed in April promises a 2 per cent year-end discount on all purchases if the dealer crosses ₹5 crore. The dealer crosses it, and the distributor issues a credit note for ₹10 lakh plus tax, linked invoice-wise. Separately, the distributor gives another dealer an unplanned ₹4 lakh goodwill discount for staying loyal in a hard year.

items.stem: On what amount does the section 50 interest run?

options.text: On the full ₹20 lakh of the liability
options.misconception: charges interest on the gross liability the way the section originally read
options.why: Gross-liability interest was the original position, litigated hard and then rewritten retrospectively. Answers citing the old position are answering a repealed law.

options.text: On nothing, since the liability was fully discharged at filing
options.misconception: treats the eventual payment as erasing the delay
options.why: The tax was due with the period's return, not four months later. Discharge ends the clock; it does not unwind it.

options.text: On the ₹14 lakh met from credit, since credit was applied late
options.misconception: inverts the proviso and charges the credit portion
options.why: The proviso protects exactly that portion. Credit sitting in the ledger was already tax paid once; charging interest on it would tax the delay twice.

options.text: On the ₹6 lakh paid through the cash ledger
options.why: The proviso to section 50(1) confines interest, where the return is filed late, to the portion discharged through the electronic cash ledger. The ₹14 lakh met by credit was the Government's money in the system all along, and Parliament amended the section retrospectively to say so.

items.scenario: A taxpayer files a GSTR-3B four months late. The tax liability of ₹20 lakh for the period was covered ₹14 lakh by input tax credit and ₹6 lakh by cash, both applied on the day of the late filing.

items.stem: What is the position in August 2026?

options.text: Neither, because goods sent for job work are not supplies at all
options.misconception: remembers the concession and forgets its condition
options.why: The tax-free movement is conditional on timely return. Break the condition and the law rewrites history — the despatch becomes a taxable supply from day one.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied in June 2026, when the year expired
options.misconception: dates the deemed supply at the breach instead of the despatch
options.why: The deeming is retrospective to the date the goods went out. That is what makes the interest bite — fourteen months of it here, not two.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied on 1 June 2025, with tax and interest; the dies have time until June 2028
options.why: Inputs get one year, and the fabric's year ran out in June 2026 — the deeming reaches back to the day of despatch, so interest runs from 2025, not from the breach. Capital goods get three years, so the dies are safely out until 2028.

options.text: Both are deemed supplied, since neither returned within one year
options.misconception: applies the inputs window to capital goods
options.why: The section keeps two clocks. Dies are capital goods on a three-year clock, and treating them on the one-year clock manufactures a liability that does not exist.

items.scenario: A manufacturer sent dies worth ₹30 lakh (capital goods) and fabric worth ₹12 lakh (inputs) to a job worker on 1 June 2025 without payment of tax. The fabric is still with the job worker in August 2026; the dies are expected back in 2027.

items.stem: Is the colleague right?

options.text: Yes, unless the exporter pays IGST on exports first and reclaims it
options.misconception: makes the pay-and-refund route the only lawful one
options.why: Paying IGST and claiming it back is one of two routes. The LUT route reaches the same destination without routing ₹18 lakh through the Government and back.

options.text: Partly — credit survives but can only offset future domestic output tax, never refund
options.misconception: allows the credit but denies the refund that makes exporting viable
options.why: An exporter with no domestic sales would accumulate credit forever. Refund of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies is the section's whole mechanism.

options.text: No — zero-rating keeps the credit alive, and the unutilised ₹18 lakh is refundable
options.why: Zero-rated is a different legal creature from exempt. Section 16 of the IGST Act preserves credit on inputs feeding zero-rated supplies, and the LUT route exists precisely so the exporter can skip charging tax yet recover the input side as a refund.

options.text: Yes — supplies on which no tax is charged are exempt, and exempt supplies block credit
options.misconception: collapses zero-rated into exempt
options.why: For exempt supplies the credit dies; for zero-rated it survives by express provision. The zero on the invoice looks identical and works oppositely, which is why the paper tests it.

items.scenario: An exporter of garments buys inputs carrying ₹18 lakh of GST and exports the entire output under a letter of undertaking, charging no tax on the export invoices. A colleague warns that selling without charging tax makes the supplies exempt, killing the input credit.

items.stem: Was an e-way bill required?

options.text: Yes — the bill attaches to movement of goods above fifty thousand rupees, sale or no sale
options.why: Rule 138 is triggered by causing movement of a consignment worth more than ₹50,000, and a branch transfer moves goods as surely as a sale does. The delivery challan takes the place of the invoice; the e-way bill is needed either way.

options.text: No, because both godowns belong to the same legal entity
options.misconception: treats intra-entity movement as outside the rule
