options.why: The standard's path runs through management first — discussion, amendment, a new report. Preventing reliance is the last resort where management refuses, not the opening move.

options.text: Discuss with management, determine whether the statements need amendment, and act on what they decide
options.why: The active search ended on 10 May, but a fact learned before issuance that would have changed the report revives the duty. The customer's insolvency on 3 May is a condition existing at the report date; if management amends, a new report follows — and if they refuse, the auditor takes steps to prevent reliance on the old one.

options.text: Note the matter in next year's audit planning as an opening-balance risk
options.misconception: defers a live reporting problem into the next cycle
options.why: The current statements are about to issue with 45 per cent of receivables owed by an insolvent customer. Next year's file is not where this year's readers get protected.

items.scenario: You signed the audit report of a company on 10 May. On 24 May, before the financial statements are issued to members, you learn that the company's largest customer — 45 per cent of receivables — filed for insolvency on 3 May.

items.stem: How should your report deal with this?

options.text: Qualified opinion, because a material uncertainty exists
options.misconception: treats the existence of uncertainty as itself a reason to modify
options.why: Adequate disclosure of an uncertainty is not a misstatement. The opinion is modified only if the disclosure is inadequate — which is the opposite of these facts.

options.text: Unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: reaches for the general emphasis paragraph where a specific required section exists
options.why: SA 570 (Revised) replaced the emphasis-paragraph treatment with a dedicated, separately headed section. Using SA 706 here omits the heading the standard requires.

options.text: Disclaimer of opinion, because the outcome cannot be predicted
options.misconception: confuses an uncertain future outcome with an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: Evidence about management's assessment was available and was obtained. SA 570 contemplates a disclaimer only in multiple-uncertainty situations of an altogether different order.

options.text: Unmodified opinion, with a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern"
options.why: SA 570 (Revised) requires exactly this when a material uncertainty exists and is adequately disclosed: the opinion stays unmodified and a separate, specifically headed section draws attention to the disclosure.

items.scenario: A client has recurring losses and a net current liability position. Management's going concern assessment concludes the entity remains a going concern, discloses the circumstances and the material uncertainty adequately in the notes, and you agree with that assessment.

items.stem: How should your report deal with this?

options.text: A qualified opinion, because a material uncertainty exists
options.misconception: modifies the opinion for an uncertainty the accounts have properly disclosed
options.why: A modification says something is wrong with the financial statements. Here they are right — they disclose the uncertainty exactly as they should. Qualifying would penalise good disclosure.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: uses the general Emphasis of Matter where the standard gives a dedicated section
options.why: Before the revision this was the treatment. SA 570 (Revised) replaced it with a section under its own heading, so that going concern uncertainty is found in the same place in every report rather than among other emphasised matters.

options.text: An adverse opinion, because the company cannot pay its debts
options.misconception: treats financial difficulty itself as a misstatement
options.why: An adverse opinion is for financial statements that are materially and pervasively wrong. A company in difficulty whose accounts say so honestly is the case for which the going concern section exists.

options.text: An unmodified opinion, with a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section drawing attention to the note
options.why: The basis is appropriate and the disclosure is adequate, so there is nothing wrong with the financial statements and the opinion stands unmodified. SA 570 (Revised) then requires a separate section under that heading, pointing to the note and stating that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.

items.scenario: A company has net current liabilities of ₹56 crore and has defaulted on a term loan. The directors have prepared the accounts on a going concern basis relying on a letter of support from the parent, and the notes describe the default, the reliance and the uncertainty in full. You are satisfied the going concern basis is appropriate but that a material uncertainty exists.

items.stem: What is wrong with relying on the representation letter here?

options.text: The letter is only valid if dated the same day as the auditor's report
options.misconception: substitutes a dating rule for the sufficiency question
options.why: Dating matters — representations are dated as near as practicable to, but not after, the date of the auditor's report — but a correctly dated letter is still not sufficient appropriate evidence on its own.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because management is responsible for the disclosures and has confirmed them in writing
options.misconception: treats management's own assertion as verification of that assertion
options.why: Management's responsibility for the financial statements is what creates the need for an audit; it does not discharge it. A representation restates the assertion under audit rather than corroborating it.

options.text: The letter should have been obtained from those charged with governance instead
options.misconception: confuses who signs the letter with what the letter can prove
options.why: Who signs it is a separate requirement, and the letter is properly requested from management with appropriate responsibilities for the financial statements. Changing the signatory would not make the representation sufficient evidence.

options.text: Written representations are never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about the matters they cover
options.why: SA 580 says this in terms. The letter is evidence, and its absence would itself be a problem, but it does not replace procedures on related parties. That management asserts something is precisely what the audit exists to test.

items.scenario: Management has signed a representation letter confirming that all related party transactions have been disclosed. You have performed no other procedures on related parties, on the basis that the letter covers the point.

items.stem: How does your audit report deal with the three branches?

options.text: It says nothing, because the principal auditor's opinion covers the whole company
options.misconception: treats silence as the way to give a single undivided opinion
options.why: The opinion does cover the whole company, and that is exactly why the division has to be disclosed. Saying nothing leaves the reader assuming the principal auditor did all of it.

options.text: It names each of the three other firms and reproduces their opinions
options.misconception: substitutes attaching other reports for stating the division
options.why: What SA 600 asks for is the magnitude of the divided portion, not a compendium of other reports. Reproducing them would not tell the reader how much of the whole they represent.

options.text: It excludes the three branches from the scope of the opinion
options.misconception: confuses dividing responsibility with limiting the scope of the opinion
options.why: The opinion is on the financial statements as a whole. Carving out branches would leave an opinion on part of a set of accounts, which is not what is being reported on.

options.text: It states the division of responsibility, giving the magnitude of the portion audited by the other auditors
options.why: SA 600 has the principal auditor disclose that part of the entity was audited by others and how large that part is. The reader then knows how much of the opinion rests on work the principal auditor did not perform.

items.scenario: You are the auditor of a company with four branches. Three are audited by other firms, whose reports you have received and reviewed. Those three branches account for 46 per cent of total assets and 39 per cent of revenue.

items.stem: To what extent may you use them to provide direct assistance?

options.text: Under your direction, supervision and review — but not for significant judgments, higher risk areas needing more than limited judgment, or work their own function has reported on
options.why: This is the revised standard's regime. Direct assistance is available once objectivity and competence are evaluated, written agreements are taken from the entity and the internal auditors, and the prohibited areas of para 30 are kept out of their hands.

options.text: Only after those charged with governance approve each procedure assigned to them
options.misconception: swaps the standard's written agreements for a per-procedure governance approval
options.why: What para 33 requires is different: one written agreement from the entity that the internal auditors may follow your instructions without interference, and one from the internal auditors on confidentiality and objectivity. Governance does not approve procedure by procedure.

options.text: Not at all — the Standard does not permit direct assistance in India
options.misconception: carries the pre-2016 position forward past the revision that reversed it
options.why: The unrevised SA 610 did not deal with direct assistance, and older study material still says India does not allow it. The revised standard, issued February 2016, contains an entire framework for it — paragraphs 26 to 35.

options.text: For any area of the audit, provided every working paper they produce is reviewed
options.misconception: treats review as curing the prohibited areas
options.why: Review is a condition, not a cure. Para 30 closes specific areas entirely — significant judgments, higher risk areas needing more than limited judgment, their own function's reported work — and no amount of review reopens them.

items.scenario: Your audit client has a competent internal audit team whose objectivity raises no significant threats. You are short-staffed and consider using two internal auditors on the audit itself.

items.stem: How should the valuer's involvement be reflected in your audit report?

options.text: Mentioned as a Key Audit Matter, since an expert was needed
options.misconception: treats the use of an expert as itself a Key Audit Matter
options.why: Key Audit Matters are the matters of most significance in the audit, selected from those communicated to those charged with governance. Engaging an expert may accompany such a matter but does not create one.

options.text: Named, with a statement that responsibility for the land valuation rests with the valuer
options.misconception: believes responsibility can be transferred to the expert by disclosing them
options.why: This is the opposite of what SA 620 says. The auditor's responsibility for the opinion is sole, and no wording in the report can move part of it to an expert.

options.text: Not mentioned at all, unless law or regulation requires it
options.why: SA 620 keeps the expert out of the report by default. Naming them invites the reader to think responsibility has been divided, when the auditor's responsibility for the opinion is undiminished.

options.text: Named in the Basis for Opinion section, to show which part of the evidence came from an expert
options.misconception: treats a reference to the expert as a helpful disclosure rather than a misleading one
options.why: A voluntary reference suggests the opinion rests partly on someone else. SA 620 permits a reference only where law or regulation requires it, and then only with a statement that it does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

items.scenario: You engage a registered valuer to value a plot of land carried at ₹22 crore. The valuer's report supports the carrying amount. You are satisfied with the valuer's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and with the reasonableness of the assumptions used.

items.stem: In what order do the first two sections of an auditor's report appear under SA 700 (Revised)?

options.text: Basis for Opinion, then Opinion
options.misconception: assumes reasons must precede a conclusion, as in the pre-revision format
options.why: This was the older shape, where the reader worked through scope and basis before reaching the opinion. The revision reversed it precisely because the opinion is what readers came for.

options.text: Management's Responsibilities, then Opinion
options.misconception: opens with whose duty it is rather than with what was concluded
options.why: The responsibilities sections sit well below the opinion and basis. Opening with them would bury the conclusion behind material the reader already assumes.

options.text: Opinion, then Basis for Opinion
options.why: The revised reporting standards deliberately put the conclusion first. Basis for Opinion follows immediately, and includes the statement that the auditor is independent and has fulfilled the other ethical responsibilities.

options.text: Key Audit Matters, then Opinion
options.misconception: promotes Key Audit Matters above the opinion itself
options.why: Key Audit Matters appear later in the report, and only where SA 701 applies. They explain what most occupied the auditor; they never displace the opinion from first position.

items.stem: For which audits is a Key Audit Matters section required?

options.text: Every audit, because the section replaces the basis-for-opinion section
options.misconception: treats key audit matters as a replacement for a section that remains required in every report
options.why: The basis-for-opinion section is required by SA 700 in all reports. Key audit matters sit alongside it and describe matters of most significance, not the basis of the opinion.

options.text: Any audit where the auditor would otherwise modify the opinion, since a key audit matter can serve instead
options.misconception: uses a key audit matter as a substitute for modifying the opinion
options.why: SA 701 states that communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for a modification when one is required by SA 705, nor for the going concern reporting required by SA 570.

options.text: Audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where law or the engagement terms otherwise require it
options.why: SA 701 applies to audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, to circumstances where the auditor is otherwise required by law or regulation to communicate key audit matters, and where the auditor decides to do so voluntarily.

options.text: Every audit, whatever the entity
options.misconception: extends a listed-entity requirement to all audits
options.why: SA 701 states its scope narrowly. For an unlisted entity the auditor may communicate key audit matters, but is not required to.

items.stem: Which opinion should you express?

options.text: Unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: uses an emphasis paragraph as a substitute for modifying the opinion
options.why: SA 706 permits an Emphasis of Matter only for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed. An uncorrected material misstatement is neither, and SA 706 expressly forbids using the paragraph in place of a modification.

options.text: Disclaimer of opinion
options.misconception: applies the inability-to-obtain-evidence branch to a known misstatement
options.why: A disclaimer addresses an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence. Here the evidence was obtained and the amount is known; the problem is that management will not correct it.

options.text: Adverse opinion
options.misconception: treats a large rupee amount as automatically pervasive
options.why: Pervasiveness is a separate test from size. SA 705 para 5 defines it by whether effects are confined to specific elements, represent a substantial proportion, or are fundamental to users' understanding — none of which the facts here establish.

options.text: Qualified opinion
options.why: The misstatement is material but confined to one line item, so it is not pervasive. SA 705 requires a qualified opinion where misstatements are material but not pervasive.

items.scenario: You are auditing a manufacturer. Inventory is overstated by ₹4.2 crore against a materiality of ₹1.1 crore. Inventory is one line item of many; the rest of the financial statements are unaffected and the misstatement does not obscure the overall picture. Management refuses to adjust.

items.stem: Which opinion should you express?

options.text: Unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter to soften a misstatement instead of modifying
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter draws attention to something properly presented in the statements. It can never be used to flag a misstatement, and using it that way is expressly ruled out.

options.text: Adverse opinion
options.why: The misstatement runs through revenue, receivables, inventory and cost of sales, so its effects are not confined to specific elements and represent a substantial proportion of the statements. That is pervasiveness, and a material and pervasive misstatement gives an adverse opinion.

options.text: Disclaimer of opinion
options.misconception: confuses a known misstatement with an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: A disclaimer is for the auditor being unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence. You have the evidence and know exactly what is wrong; the problem is the accounting, not access to information.

options.text: Qualified opinion
options.misconception: reaches for a qualification without testing whether the effects are confined
options.why: A qualification is for misstatements that are material but not pervasive. Here the wrong policy touches most of the primary statement, which is the condition the adverse opinion exists for.

items.scenario: You are auditing a company whose entire revenue recognition policy is wrong: it recognises revenue on despatch of goods held on consignment, which are not yet sold. Revenue, receivables, inventory, cost of sales and every ratio derived from them are affected. Management will not change the policy.

items.stem: Which paragraphs do these two matters call for?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph for the tax dispute and an Other Matter paragraph for the predecessor auditor
options.why: SA 706 (Revised) uses an Emphasis of Matter for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and an Other Matter for a matter not so disclosed that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report. The tax dispute is disclosed; the predecessor auditor is not.

options.text: Either paragraph will do for either matter, since the two are interchangeable
options.misconception: treats two paragraphs with different defined uses as interchangeable
options.why: The distinction is whether the matter appears in the financial statements. An Emphasis of Matter must refer to something disclosed there, so it cannot carry the predecessor auditor point.

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph for both, including the undisclosed predecessor auditor
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter for a matter the financial statements do not disclose
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter draws attention to a disclosure. Where there is no disclosure to point at, the paragraph has nothing to emphasise.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph for both, which also modifies the opinion
options.misconception: believes an Other Matter paragraph modifies the opinion
options.why: Neither paragraph modifies the opinion. SA 706 (Revised) states that both are used for matters other than those presented or disclosed that are materially misstated, and modification is governed by SA 705.

items.scenario: The financial statements disclose, in a note, an ongoing tax dispute whose outcome could be significant. Separately, the prior year's financial statements were audited by another firm, a fact not disclosed anywhere in the financial statements.

items.stem: How does your opinion treat the previous year's figures?

options.text: The opinion covers the current period only, and does not refer to the corresponding figures
options.why: Figures shown alongside the current period for context are corresponding figures. They are an integral part of the current period's statements and are read only in relation to it, so the opinion does not extend to them as a separate period.

options.text: The opinion covers neither period until the prior year's auditor confirms their figures
options.misconception: makes the current opinion conditional on the predecessor auditor
options.why: Nothing in SA 710 makes the opinion wait on another auditor. Where the prior period was audited by someone else, that fact is stated in an Other Matter paragraph and the current opinion is given as normal.

options.text: The opinion covers the current period, and a separate paragraph gives an opinion on the prior period
options.misconception: invents a second opinion where the standard gives one
options.why: There is no such paragraph. Where a prior-period matter needs raising — for instance a previously modified opinion still unresolved — it is dealt with in the current opinion or in an Other Matter paragraph, not a second opinion.

options.text: The opinion covers both periods separately, since both sets of amounts are presented
options.misconception: treats any presented comparative as a comparative financial statement
options.why: That is the treatment for comparative financial statements, where each period is presented as a full set for its own sake. Corresponding figures are not that, and SA 710 keeps the two apart deliberately.

items.scenario: A company presents its balance sheet and statement of profit and loss for the year ended 31 March 2026 with the previous year's amounts shown alongside as comparatives, in the form required by Schedule III. The comparatives are not separately headed as a second set of financial statements.

items.stem: What does SA 720 require you to do?

options.text: Nothing, because the MD&A is not part of the audited financial statements
options.misconception: reads "not audited" as "not the auditor's concern"
options.why: The auditor expresses no opinion on the other information, but SA 720 still requires reading it and acting on inconsistencies. Not auditing it is not the same as ignoring it.

options.text: Treat it as an uncorrected material inconsistency and describe it in the Other Information section of your report
options.why: Reading the other information and identifying inconsistencies with the audited statements is exactly the responsibility SA 720 creates. Where management will not correct one, the auditor describes the uncorrected inconsistency in the Other Information section.

options.text: Express a qualified conclusion on the Management Discussion and Analysis
options.misconception: invents an opinion on other information that SA 720 expressly does not give
options.why: There is no opinion or conclusion on other information at all. The Other Information section says so in terms, and then describes any uncorrected inconsistency.

options.text: Modify the opinion on the financial statements
options.misconception: modifies the opinion for something outside the financial statements
options.why: The financial statements are right; the MD&A is wrong. Modifying the opinion would tell readers the audited figures cannot be relied on, which is false and is not what SA 720 asks for.

items.scenario: The annual report contains a Management Discussion and Analysis stating that exports grew by 31 per cent during the year. The audited financial statements disclose export revenue that has grown by 12 per cent. Management declines to change the figure in the MD&A.
